13900-collected-poems-1897-1907-by-henry:
Henry Newbolt collected his poems from 1897 to 1907 in this volume, dedicated to Thomas Hardy. Drake's Drum opens the book, with Drake asleep in his hammock a thousand miles away, dreaming of Plymouth Hoe. Sailor lads dance, shore lights flash, and night tides dash in the famous refrain. Other poems follow fleets, soldiers, and English history.

Newbolt writes stirring verse on duty, empire, and the sea. A later poem watches the Straits open wide, with hearts dancing like the sea as the French sail for Martinique. The collection captures Edwardian patriotic poetry at its peak. Modern readers may find its imperial tone dated, yet its music endures. It remains Newbolt's best-known gathering.
14244-the-romance-of-tristan-and-iseult:
Joseph Bédier retold the romance of Tristan and Iseult from the best French sources, and H. Belloc rendered it into English in 1913. Crowned by the French Academy, the tale opens with Tristan's childhood, the Morholt out of Ireland, and the quest for the lady with hair of gold. A philtre binds the lovers, and the tall pine tree, the discovery, and the chantry leap follow.

Exile and ordeal deepen the story. In the wood of Morois, Ogrin the hermit shelters the pair, while Brangien devises subtle ruses to save them. Iseult dreams of scythes and traps cutting her knees, and blood upon the ground. King Mark, pressed by barons, exiles Tristan, then drives the barons themselves from his land when they fall silent. Madness, a second Iseult of the White Hands, and death close the romance. Love and fate, told simply, still overwhelm.
17178-westerfelt:
Will N. Harben's 1901 novel opens at a quilting in a mountain home, where two sisters and their neighbors sew a bright, varicolored square and gossip the day away. Mrs. Slogan, childless and past sixty, praises the quilt as the prettiest yet, while her softer sister Mrs. Dawson irons out its wrinkles. The sun sets behind the mountain as the workers leave by field and wood paths.

From this homely start Harben builds a southern mountain tale of kin, pride, and love, told in dialect speech and close home detail. The quilting scene sets the book's tone: plain folk, sharp talk, and strong feeling under a quiet roof. Readers who like regional novels will enjoy its slow, vivid opening and its mountain world.
22352-american-boy-s-life-of-theodore-ro:
Edward Stratemeyer's American Boys' Life of Theodore Roosevelt came out in 1904. It told the president's life for young readers. A plate shows Colonel Roosevelt at San Juan Hill, his famous battle.

Stratemeyer had already written an American boys' life of William McKinley. He also produced the Old Glory and Pan-American series for boys. This volume fits that pattern of patriotic biography. Boys were offered Roosevelt as soldier, leader, and example. The book shows how a sitting president was packaged as a hero for youth. Readers today can study both Roosevelt's image and the boys' book trade at once.
23810-at-fault:
Kate Chopin's At Fault opens on a Louisiana plantation of four thousand acres, left unencumbered to Thérèse Lafirme. When her husband Jérôme dies suddenly, neighbors watch with indolent interest, expecting some folly from a handsome, inconsolable, childless Creole widow of thirty.

The folly fails to appear. Thérèse follows her husband's methods so successfully that the only wonder is her competence. Around her move Melicent, Fanny, and the household of Place-du-Bois, through pine woods, pirogues, and painful disclosures. Chopin's novel studies a widow's independence, a sister's talk, and the slow, fateful working of fault and forgiveness.
29021-the-fairy-tales-of-charles-perraul:
Charles Perrault's fairy tales appear here in the edition illustrated by Harry Clarke, with an introduction by Thomas Bodkin, first published by Harrap in London in August 1922. The contents run from Little Red Riding-Hood and The Fairy through Blue Beard and The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood to The Master Cat, or Puss in Boots. Cinderilla, Riquet with the Tuft, Little Thumb, and Donkey-Skin follow.

Clarke's pictures, including Cinderilla and her prince as frontispiece, dress the old tales in rich, strange art. Bodkin's introduction sets Perrault's stories in their French classic form. Readers get the best-known fairy tales of Europe in a handsome edition, suited to reading aloud and to keeping, with pictures that match the tales' wonder and menace.
29312-camping-with-president-roosevelt:
John Burroughs published this account in 1906, reprinted from The Atlantic Monthly of May 1906, of his camping trip to Yellowstone Park with President Theodore Roosevelt in the spring of 1903. Burroughs had promised friends to write up his impressions of the president and the park, though he was slow to get around to it. Roosevelt himself, Burroughs jokes, wrote his account nearly two years earlier from the leisure of the White House.

Chapters cover the president's interest in natural history, his love of animals, meeting the people, cowboy friends, ranch life, and the Bad Lands and bad men. Readers get a naturalist's portrait of a president outdoors, warm and observant, from the days when Yellowstone itself was still a wild frontier.
31055-twenty-five-years-in-the-black-bel:
William J. Edwards wrote this 1918 memoir, published by the Cornhill Company in Boston, with pictures. It is dedicated to his loving wife, who encouraged him in all his early struggles and aided him in all his achievements. Edwards, a Tuskegee graduate, tells twenty-five years of work in the Black Belt, from childhood days to the founding of a school.

Twenty chapters run from Childhood Days, Shadows, and A Ray of Light through Life at Tuskegee and Reconnoitering to Founding the Snow Hill School and Small Beginnings. Later chapters cover campaigning for funds in the North, the origin of the Jeanes Fund, graduates and ex-students, the Negro exodus, and the Negro and the public schools of the South. They end with the Negro and the World War. It is a frank, inspiring account of Black education in the South.
33053-camping-tramping-with-roosevelt:
John Burroughs's Camping and Tramping with Roosevelt records the naturalist's trip with President Theodore Roosevelt to Yellowstone Park. It was written in the fall of 1905 after Roosevelt had already published his own account nearly two years earlier. Burroughs, at his home Slabsides, explains that he knew he would be in a storm center, since Roosevelt's abounding energy set everything in motion wherever he went. He feared snow six and seven feet deep where travel meant snowshoes.

Once the crowds and speeches were over, the two men were alone in the park wilderness with only a superintendent and a few attendants. Burroughs found the president at his most vivid. The book is both a nature memoir and a portrait of Roosevelt in the field, watching birds, beasts, and geysers with a naturalist's patience beside a president's restlessness. It remains a warm, first-hand glimpse of two famous Americans outdoors.
4252-theodore-roosevelt:
Edmund Lester Pearson wrote this short life of Theodore Roosevelt for the True Stories of Great Americans series. Macmillan published it in 1920, a year after Roosevelt's death. Pearson drew on Roosevelt's own writings for the story. He also drew on William Roscoe Thayer's intimate biography.

The chapters trace a path from a sickly boy to soldier, governor, and president. They cover his ranching years and his service in the Spanish-American War. They cover his White House years and his later travels and writing. Written close to its subject's lifetime, the book gives young readers a clear, admiring outline.
43875-the-boy-chums-in-the-florida-jungl:
Wilmer M Ely wrote The Boy Chums in the Florida Jungle, a boys’ adventure tale. A L Burt Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred fifteen. Ely had written six Boy Chums tales before this one. Charlie West and Walter Hazard stand at its heart, deep among the Seminole Indians.

Chris, a small Black boy, opens the tale at a bridge, fishing. Fish crowd his hook but will not bite, to his disgust. The chums soon run an engine and camp in wild woods. A convicts’ camp, a strike, and a crew change crowd the middle chapters. Fire must be fought in the dry jungle brush. A medicine man, an old fort, and a hidden voice raise the stakes. The riddle clears at last, and a buyer takes the whole outfit.
44733-an-introduction-to-the-prose-and-p:
Hiram Corson wrote an intro to Milton's prose and verse works. The Macmillan Company issued it at New York in 1899. Corson taught English literature at Cornell University. The book holds all of Milton's self-told passages. His clearest words on true liberty join them. Comus, Lycidas, and Samson Agonistes print in full.

Notes and forewords guide the reader through. A Paradise Lost motto heads the whole. Servant of God, well done, it opens. Milton fought the better fight alone, it says. Reproach from all the world was his wage. A Tennyson-like praise of Milton's organ voice follows. Mighty-mouthed inventor of harmonies, it calls him. A professor's doorway into Milton joins the poet's own life words to his three great shorter works for class and home.
47035-the-history-of-salt:
The History of Salt is a treatise by Evan Marlett Boddy, a London surgeon and fellow of learned societies. It came out in London in 1881. Boddy treats salt as far more than a thing for the table.

Nine chapters cover salt in old times and salt as a drug and a poison. He traces where salt is found and how it forms in the earth. Later chapters weigh its effects on plants, beasts and men. He closes with its uses in food and in health. The book gives a plain, full account of a common but key substance. An appendix rounds out the facts and sources for keen readers.
51831-my-brother-theodore-roosevelt:
Corinne Roosevelt Robinson published My Brother Theodore Roosevelt in New York in 1921, two years after the former president's death. She states plainly that the book is not a biography and not a political history. It is a sister's set of personal recollections, checked against letters and memory, offered to a public that loved him and that he loved in return.

She calls her brother the Great Sharer, a man who shared his goods, his mind, his sympathy, and his fun with everyone near him, above all with his family. The dedication honors their sister Anna, whose devotion to Theodore never wavered. A front picture shows Roosevelt with his little granddaughter in 1918. Contents begin in the nursery and move through green fields and foreign years into his public life. Readers get the president as his youngest sister knew him, at close hand and in tender detail.
52719-four-and-twenty-fairy-tales-select:
Planché chose and turned into English a set of French fairy tales. The book came out in London in 1858. It holds tales by Perrault and by other French writers of his time. Planché says he took the tales from the Cabinet des Fées. He gave the book to his daughter, a writer of tales for the young.

Inside are Blue Beard, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots, and Cinderella. Later tales add Beauty and the Beast and Prince Chéri. Notes sit with the tales to aid the reader. The order runs from old writers to new. Readers get classic tales in full form.
59521-salt-or-no-salt:
Salt or No Salt, America's new table seasoning, is a booklet from the Sunkist kitchen. Its case is fresh lemon juice, used at the table in place of or beside salt. Lemons have long been a standard flavoring for pies, tomato juice, tea, fish, and sea food, the booklet opens. Now millions are finding that a squeeze of fresh lemon lifts a long list of other foods as well.

The new habit began, it says, with the thousands of people on low-salt and slimming diets. Their real problem was to find a table seasoning to make up for the loss of salt. A squeeze of lemon brings out the food's own flavors, it holds. A list of foods runs from soups, salads, and fish to roasts, melons, and desserts. Serve a dish of lemon wedges on the table at every meal, the booklet urges.
6075-miss-gibbie-gault:
Kate Langley Bosher, author of Mary Cary, opens Miss Gibbie Gault with the Needlework Guild, meeting Thursdays at eleven, this time with Mrs. Tate for the last gathering before summer adjournment. Mrs. Pryor, the president, has personally requested a large attendance, and gossip, the guild's true business, hums along.

Chapters follow the views of Miss Gibbie, apple-blossom land, a council chamber, Mary Cary speaking, midnight, Peggy and her party, and a forgotten engagement. A bargain, a grateful convalescent, a testimony party, and a surrender follow. Bosher writes warm small-town comedy, where talk shapes fates.
61110-tybalt:
Tybalt, by Stephen Barr, was printed from Worlds of If Science Fiction of March 1962. A head note calls youth a perilous time, for a man or for the whole race of man. A physics teacher rubs his board clean at the end of class, and finds one pupil still at his desk.

Howard Dax is a precise man, vexed by one boy in his class. Mallison is thin and fifteen, with long dark hair and pointed side whiskers. His face hints at a sneer that never quite lands. He asks, in a calm, adult tone, why Dax does not like him, and why his grades run low. Dax holds that the boy does not try, though he could do far better. Fans get a tense talk of youth, pride, and a mind past its years.
64052-tonight-the-stars-revolt:
Gardner Fox writes a sword and planet novel in Tonight the Stars Revolt, from the March 1952 issue of Planet Stories. The head blurb tells of Black Pools that hold the lost wisdom of the Ancients, lost for fifty thousand years. Red Angus held victory in his sword hand for one day.

The pools gape like the mouth of space, dark and deep past guess. Some say a god dwells in them, some say they are the hollow core of the world. One man of fifty thousand years knows their secret from a hidden city. Red Angus flees through the alleys of the Lower City. A fresh brand on his shoulder marks him a pirate, and the Citadel guard hunts him.
64402-the-reign-of-gilt:
The Reign of Gilt, by David Graham Phillips, was published in New York in nineteen oh five by James Pott and Company. The first impression is dated September of that year. Phillips divides his indictment into two parts: plutocracy and democracy. Seventeen chapters carry the argument from the mania for gilt to the real American woman.

The opening quotes the Episcopal bishop of New York on his own flock. Young girls of the triumphant classes, the bishop says, have their price like slaves in a market. The rich buy legislatures as their highest distinction, he charges. Phillips answers with chapters on democracy's dynamo and the inevitable ideal. Not generosity but justice is his remedy's name. The book is muckraking in essay form, aimed at the made-over White House and the pauper-making rich.
65809-christmas-at-sagamore-hill-with-th:
Helen Topping Miller wrote Christmas at Sagamore Hill with Theodore Roosevelt. Longmans, Green and Company issued it in 1960. The book came out in Canada at the same time. Its Congress card number reads 60-53227. A bitter cold night opens the tale. Raw wind blows off the Bay that night.

Dry leaves scud under that wind at the start. Roosevelt steps down from his carriage with care. He holds both arms straight out before him. A great globe of goldfish rides in them. A thin film of ice skins the water there. Fish dash in hysterics inside the globe. He walks firm as in Cuba's hills, she writes. No one shoots at him now, he thinks with thanks. A warm imagined Christmas at the great man's house was built for young readers who loved his legend.
66081-the-vault:
Murray Leinster tells a tale of a night thief at work in a jewelry factory. Mike, the intruder, finds a window that slides up too easily and waits long in the dark before moving. The great plant of the Whitney Jewelry and Watch Company stands still, lit only by a dim lamp at the gate.

Inside, Mike moves like a moth through the corridors, noting smells of oil, paint, and fresh-mopped floors. He times his steps by the watchman's round, creaking shoes and lantern marking the man's slow path. His goal is the huge vault on the second floor, where all the firm's precious stock sleeps at night. Readers get a taut study of patience, nerve, and craft on the wrong side of the law.
67722-condensed-history-of-the-mexican-w:
Condensed History of the Mexican War and Its Glorious Results is a veterans' souvenir volume. John E Cowan compiled and published it in New York, at 25 cents. The first edition ran to 25,000 copies. The history is by the Hon William McKay of the Palmetto Regiment. Reminiscences follow from Colonel Daniel E Hungerford and Colonel Chas J Murphy.

An errata note opens the book on a comic quarrel. Murphy learned that comrade James C Carleton was born on June 17, 1832. Murphy himself was born on June 3 of the same year. So Murphy is not, after all, the youngest veteran of the war. He takes his hat off to Carleton and moves to a back seat. The history proper began as a banquet speech. Veterans met at the Hotel Continental in Paris. They celebrated September 14, 1847, the fall of Mexico's capital.
67869-love-conquers-pride-or-where-peace:
Miller wrote a love tale for a cheap reprint series sold at fifteen cents a volume. The New Eagle list held hundreds of such tales, by Sheldon, Garvice, Fleming, and others. The volumes ran from two hundred fifty six to three hundred twenty pages, in good type.

The tale's own name promises its plot in brief. Pride stands in the way of love, and love must beat it down before peace can dwell where the pair live. Miller was a staple of this list. Such books were the light reading of their day, sold cheap and read fast. The front pages of this copy are given to the whole catalogue.
70647-the-belt:
Wallace West opens with theory in The Belt, from the November 1951 issue of Science Fiction Quarterly. Scientific theories are never true or false, the head piece argues. They are good or bad in various degrees, and the test is usefulness. A theory may be discarded simply because another accounts for the phenomena more simply.

The tale turns to an island experiment. No one foresaw what would come of the social experiment Jonathan Robertson started early in the eighteenth century, it says. Jonathan the seventh found the terrible fruit of what had been sown. A ship's captain spits over the rail into blue waters: rum port to come home to, he calls New Patmos. The name gives him the jumps, he owns, thinking of Saint John's hard exile on the first Patmos.
70696-stella-rosevelt:
Stella Rosevelt is a novel by Georgie Sheldon, in an edition copyrighted in 1883 and 1890. Dillingham published the book at New York, the copyright resting with Street and Smith. Sheldon is named as author of Brownie Triumph, The Forsaken Bride, and Earle Wayne Nobility. Contents list twenty chapters and more for the tale of her heroine.

On the Atlantic, Saved, and The Young Stranger open the story in order of the chapters. Mrs Richards, Bitter Disappointment, and Stella Appeal follow in the list of the book. A Consultation, Retrenchment, and Change of Fortune carry her into a new world in turn. The Unwelcome Guest, Filthy Lucre, and The Cameo Ring fill the middle chapters. Sheldon wrote for the story papers, where her heroines pass from shipwreck to fortune by way of rings, shocks, and explanations.
71360-nobody-s-fault:
Netta Syrett wrote a novel printed in Boston and London in 1896. A verse from Matthew Arnold fronts the book, of freed prisoners who sail the wide ocean of life anew. The tale opens in a London square in dismal November fog. Mrs Trelawney's drawing room glows by contrast, with clear fire and shaded lamps.

Her husband jokes that Stevens is never busy, as Stevens leans back in an armchair. Talk turns to a woman's book by a writer named Bridget Ruan, not the usual woman's novel, one man says with praise to heaven. Love, art, work, and blame move through drawing rooms as the title asks who, if any one, is at fault.
7360-the-tryal-of-william-penn-william-m:
The Tryal of William Penn and William Mead for causing a tumult records the Old Bailey sessions of September 1, 3, 4, and 5, 1670. It was done by themselves and transcribed from the Compleat Collection of State Tryals first published in 1719, edited by Don Seitz. Seitz dedicates the volume to the memory of Thomas Jefferson, which needs frequent refreshing. His foreword praises Penn, the Quaker, for coming nearer than any other human being to establishing liberty, equality, and fraternity as a living ideal.

Penn's courtroom stand for conscience and jury freedom gives the trial its lasting fame. The old record lets readers hear the clash of judge, jury, and prisoner in its own words. This text preserves a founding moment of religious liberty and trial by jury.
77791-the-peyote-cult:
The Peyote Cult is a study of the Native American peyote religion by Weston La Barre, professor of anthropology at Duke University. It first appeared as number 19 of the Yale University Publications in Anthropology. The text here is the 1959 reprint by the Shoe String Press of Hamden, Connecticut, issued with Yale's leave.

La Barre thanks Edward Sapir, Clark Wissler, and others who funded and guided the field work behind the book. His note to the reprint says that in the twenty years since first publication, studies of peyotism kept appearing. Over one thousand items on the subject then existed. The book stands as a founding study of the peyote rite and its spread.
79242-the-price-of-salt:
The Price of Salt is a 1952 novel issued under the name Claire Morgan. Coward-McCann published it first, and Bantam Books reprinted it in 1953. The book is dedicated to Edna, Jordy, and Jeff. Its pages quote a popular song and lines from a poem by Eliot.

An early scene shows Carol drawing Therese close and kissing her hair. The first chapter opens at Frankenberg's store during the lunch rush. The staff cafeteria is packed, and more workers keep arriving with trays. Therese is part of this busy store world. The novel follows the close bond that grows between Therese and Carol. Their scenes carry a charge that the opening kiss makes plain.
9631-waltoniana-inedited-remains-in-vers:
Richard Herne Shepherd edited Waltoniana in 1878, gathering unprinted remains of Izaak Walton, author of The Compleat Angler. The book spans 1633 to 1673, from an elegy on Dr. Donne to dedications, prefaces, and letters. Pieces include lines on Donne's portrait, verses for a merchants' map, and a preface to Quarles. An epitaph for Walton's second wife Anne Ken also appears.

Shepherd's notes and preface place each scrap in Walton's long life among poets and divines. The remains show Walton as friend, churchman, and angler, not just a single book's author. A reader gets a rare, intimate Walton, in small pieces that light up seventeenth-century English letters.
britannica-1911-anhalt:
Anhalt is a duchy of Germany. It forms a constituent state of the German empire. Two older duchies merged to create it in 1863. Those were Anhalt-Dessau-Cöthen and Anhalt-Bernburg. The territory splits into eastern and western parts. A strip of Prussian Saxony separates them. Five small enclaves also lie inside Prussian ground. The western part reaches into the Harz range. The Ramberg peak rises there to 1,900 feet.

From the Harz, land shelves gently toward the Saale. Fertile tracts lie between the Saale and Elbe. The long entry surveys rivers, towns, and products. It also traces the dynasty's tangled partitions since 1603. German documentary collections anchor the closing bibliography. Siebigk's statistical history of the duchy appears there. So does a multi-volume diplomatic codex. The article suits readers tracing small German states before unification settled their map.
britannica-1911-asphalt:
Asphalt, or asphaltum, is the solid or half-solid kind of bitumen, treated in this 1911 Britannica article. The Greeks called it asphaltos, and the asphalt of the Dead Sea drew notice from early travellers. People of the lands around gathered it, Diodorus says, for use in Egypt in preserving the dead.

Like other forms of bitumen, asphalt is found widely, in rocks of all ages. The article holds that the chief deposits come from liquid petroleum that has escaped from rock layers and then dried and thickened in the air. The famed Pitch Lake of Trinidad, long thought the largest deposit of all, covers 99.3 acres and is firm enough in places to bear a team of horses. It is worked with picks to a foot or two deep, and the holes soon fill again from below.
britannica-1911-assault:
Assault is the subject of a law entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Latin terms for leaping upon a person. In English law it means an attempt or offer to do bodily hurt by force. Striking at a person with a stick counts, even if the blow misses.

The entry makes clear that mere words, however harsh, do not make an assault. With the threat there must be the means to carry it out at once. Battery is set apart as the next step beyond assault. In battery the hurt has in fact been done to the person. That line between threat and act is the core of the entry.
britannica-1911-bagillt:
Bagillt is a town of Flintshire in North Wales, on the London and North Western railway in the old parish of Holywell, with 2,637 people in 1901. Its weight comes from industry: zinc, lead, iron, and alkali works, with kindred trades and collieries around it.

Above the town rises Bryn Dychwelwch, the Hill of Retreat, named for Owen Gwynedd's escape there from Henry II's larger force. Nearby stands Mostyn Hall, seat of one of the oldest Welsh families since Henry VI's time, holding antiquities and old Welsh manuscripts, a harp dated 1568, and golden torques. Henry VII, then earl of Richmond, is said to have hidden at Mostyn from Richard III, sheltered by its lord.
britannica-1911-basalt:
Basalt, in petrology, the study of rocks, is treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name may come from an Ethiopian word for a stone yielding iron; Pliny placed the first basalts in Ethiopia. In modern use it covers dark igneous rocks, formed from molten material, that are rich in magnesia and iron and weather to brown. Some basalts are largely glassy, many fine grained, and many show larger crystals in a finer ground.

Minerals and structure carry the detail. Olivine and pitch-black augite are the commonest large crystals, with plagioclase felspar also frequent. Cooling lava often split into striking columns, the famous basaltic jointing. Steam holes in the rock later filled with calcite, chlorite, and zeolites. Older altered basalts went by names such as diabase and melaphyre, while trap served as a general term. Werner's water-born origin and Hutton's volcanic one are also recalled.
britannica-1911-belt:
Belt is a word shared by the Teutonic tongues, from an old German form that probably gave Latin its balteus. At root it is a flat strap of leather or other stuff worn as a girdle. The sword-belt in particular served as the chief ornament when an earl or knight was invested.

In machinery a belt is the flexible strap that runs round drums, pulleys or wheels to carry power from one to another. The word then spreads by shape: any broad stripe takes the name, from the bands on Jupiter to a warship’s armour at the water-line. Even a long, narrow tract of land with marked traits, like an earthquake-belt, borrows it.
britannica-1911-bolt:
Bolt is a word entry that starts from an Old English term for a crossbow shaft, a quarrel, and for the pin that fastened a door. From the arrow's swift flight comes the verb to bolt, said of a running horse, and phrases like bolt upright. American speech added the sense of a voter bolting his own party's chosen man.

As a fastening pin the word spread to many devices. A bolt of cloth, a set length in a roll such as 40 feet of canvas, takes its name from things fastened together. A second, unrelated bolt means to sift, from an Old French verb. Shakespeare and Burke are quoted for that use, and Milton for bolting as sifting out an argument in debate.
britannica-1911-catapult:
Catapult was a broad name for war engines of crossbow type in the ancient world. A 1911 Britannica entry traces when such engines first came into wide use. Greek armies of the fifth century before Christ seem to have had none. The first large siege train on record dates to 399, when Dionysius of Syracuse armed against Carthage.

From Sicily the engines spread to Greece and were used by Philip of Macedon at Byzantium. Roman engines kept the same Greek forms in the main. Small catapults shot arrows on a flat path, like direct fire today. Large ballistae threw heavy bolts or stones on a high arc, much like a howitzer.
britannica-1911-chatellerault:
Châtellerault is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Vienne. It stands on the right bank of the Vienne, 19 miles north north east of Poitiers. Its population in 1906 was 15,214. A stone bridge of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries links it to the suburb of Châteauneuf. Massive towers guard the bridge's western end.

Cutlery is made on a large scale in villages along the Clain, south of the town. The other great works is the national small arms factory at Châteauneuf, set up in 1815. It employs from 1500 to 5500 men. The town's name comes from a fortress built in the tenth century by Airaud, viscount of the territory. In 1515 it was made a duchy for François de Bourbon, but it soon returned to the crown. In 1548 it was bestowed on James Hamilton, earl of Arran.
britannica-1911-clermont-l-herault:
Clermont-l'Hérault, or Clermont de Lodève, is a town of southern France in Hérault, ten miles south-south-east by rail of Lodève, with 4,731 people in 1906. It is built on the slope of a hill crowned by an ancient castle. The Rhonel, a tributary of the Lergue, skirts the town below that hill. An interesting church of the 13th and 14th centuries stands among its buildings.

Cloth for military clothing and woollen goods form the chief manufacture, an industry dating from the latter half of the 17th century. Tanning and leather dressing are also carried on in the town. Trade in wine, wool and grain supports it beyond those workshops. Public institutions include a tribunal of commerce, a chamber of arts and manufactures and a communal college. The town was several times taken and retaken in the religious wars of the 16th century.
britannica-1911-default:
Default, in English law, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from French roots for a failure. In law it means a failure to do an act that the law calls for. The act may be a set step in a suit, or a duty laid on a person by law.

A party to a suit falls in default by not showing up or by not taking a step in the set time. The other side then gains ground and may sign judgment. As a rule the price of default is an order to pay the costs it caused. Where a judgment is not obeyed, the cure is to carry it out by the means the law allows. In fine cases a court may order prison if the fine is not paid.
britannica-1911-faribault:
Only the closing portion of the Faribault article is hosted here; the text opens mid-sentence, and its earlier part is not present. What survives describes an American city with a public library and its own water-supply system. Good water power serves manufactures of flour, beer, shoes, furniture, pianos and woollen goods. The city took its name from Jean Baptiste Faribault, a French fur-trader who made his headquarters in the region in the late 18th century.

Permanent settlement came about 1848, and the city was chartered in 1872. About 1860 the French millwright N. La Croix brought in a flour process that reshaped the industry in the United States. A flood wrecked his mill, and the process first succeeded at scale in Minneapolis. Bishop Henry Benjamin Whipple, pioneer Episcopal bishop in Minnesota from 1850 to 1901, made the city his home for many years. His missionary work among the Indians is noted.
britannica-1911-fault:
Fault, in its general sense, is a failing, mistake or defect, a word reaching English through French from Latin fallere, to fail. In geology, the entry's main subject, a fault is a plane of dislocation in the earth's crust. Mining synonyms include trouble, throw and heave. Movement of rock on one side of the plane against the other is what sets a fault apart from a joint or fissure.

Some faults are clean-cut planes, as if rock had been sliced and refitted after shifting. More often the rocks near the plane are bent, broken and crumpled into a belt of fault-rock. The entry explains fault lines, minor faults branching from a main one, thrusts and lag faults, using figures throughout. It notes that faults occur in rocks of all ages. Sudden yielding along a fault plane, it adds, is a familiar cause of earthquakes.
britannica-1911-felt:
Felt is the subject of a cloth entry in the 1911 Britannica. Felt is a cloth made by matting fibres close together. Wool, hair, and fur are the chief stuffs used. Most fibres mat to some degree when worked. Only wool, fur, and some hairs felt well in full. Scale shape and curl of those fibres cause the grip. Wool must be added to carry fibres that will not felt.

Two classes of felt are set out in the entry. One class is woven first and then felted hard. Its yarn is spun and woven with care for that end. It is then scoured, milled, dyed, and finished like cloth. Light kinds use one cloth and heavy kinds use more. The second class is true felt with no weave at all. Its past is held to reach back before spinning came.
britannica-1911-fontevrault:
Fontevrault, or Fontevraud, is a town of western France in the department of Maine-et-Loire. It stands ten miles south-east of Saumur by road, amid the forest of Fontevrault, and had 1,279 people in 1906. The interest of the place centres in its abbey. Since 1804 that abbey has been used as a central house of detention for convicts. Its twelfth-century church keeps only its choir and apse for divine service, under a fifth cupola above the crossing.

In a chapel of the south transept lie the effigies of English kings and queens. Henry II of England, his wife Eleanor of Guienne, Richard I and Isabella of Angouleme, wife of John, rest there. Eleanor's figure is in oak and the rest in stone. The cloister, refectory and chapter-house date from the sixteenth century. The entry tours the abbey buildings and their prison use.
britannica-1911-fourchambault:
Fourchambault is a town of central France in the department of Nievre. It stands on the right bank of the Loire, four and a half miles north-west of Nevers, on the Paris-Lyon railway. Its population in 1906 was 4,591. The town owes its importance to its great iron-works, established in 1821. They employ 2,000 workmen and produce engineering material for railway, military and other purposes, a single industry large enough to shape the whole life and growth of the place beside the river.

Among its masterpieces are the metal parts of the Pont du Carrousel in Paris and the iron beams of Chartres cathedral's roof. Its works also built the bridge over the Dordogne at Cubzac. A small canal joins the works to the Lateral canal of the Loire. The short entry portrays a company town and its one great works.
britannica-1911-galt:
Galt is a town in Waterloo county, Ontario, Canada, on the Grand river. The 1911 Britannica entry places it 23 miles north-north-west of Hamilton, served by both the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific railways. Its population rose from 5,187 in 1881 to 7,866 in 1901.

The town is named after John Galt, the author. The entry stresses its strong water power, drawn from the river, which drives flour-mills. Its factories make edge tools, castings, machinery, paper and other goods. The notice is a compact gazetteer entry: position, growth, name and industry, in a handful of lines.
britannica-1911-gault:
Gault, in the 1911 Britannica geology entry, is a stiff blue clay forming one member of the Lower Cretaceous system. The name is also used in parts of England for any stiff blue clay, and older writers spelt it Galt or Golt. In the south of England the Gault clay lies between two sandy beds, the Upper and Lower Greensands.

Because the clay turns sandy as it is traced, and its fossils match those of the Upper Greensand, Jukes-Browne proposed treating both as one formation, the Selbornian. The entry sets out that scheme, with the rock types it covers, from blue marls to the Red Chalk of Yorkshire. It then gives the Selbornian's divisions with their marker fossils, and maps the outcrop round the Weald and under the London basin.
britannica-1911-glauber-s-salt:
Glauber's salt is a form of sodium sulphate that holds ten parts of water. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says it was first set out by Glauber in 1658. He made it by pouring oil of vitriol on common salt. He praised its healing powers and called it his wondrous salt. As a mineral it occurs in Spain, North America, and the Caucasus. A thick bed of the pure salt lies near Tiflis.

It is the working part of many spa waters and occurs in sea water and blood. Its taste is bitter and salty but not sharp. It forms large clear prisms that crumble in dry air. At blood heat it melts in its own water. Past that point its power to dissolve falls as heat rises. The entry gives the mix of the pure salt in dry figures.
britannica-1911-indult: Indult is a brief church law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term meaning to grant or allow. An indult is a licence from the pope. It lets a person do a thing that the common law of the church does not allow. The entry gives one clear case as its example. By an indult the pope may let a bishop grant eased rules for the Lenten fast. The easing is shaped to fit the needs of the place, its climate, and its state.
britannica-1911-microcosmic-salt:
Microcosmic Salt is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a chemical salt. It is ammonium sodium hydrogen phosphate in full naming. Alchemists gave it its odd name for a reason. It is contained in the decomposing urine of man, the microcosm. It is of historical interest for one great link. Brand prepared phosphorus from this raw material long ago. Hence it is also called salt of phosphorus.

It can be gained in large transparent crystals by mixing. Solutions of sal-ammoniac and disodium phosphate give those crystals. It can also be made by treating a phosphate solution with ammonia. When heated to redness, it leaves a clear glass. That glass is sodium metaphosphate in the text. Like borax, it dissolves most metallic oxides in heat. The glasses formed often show characteristic colours. That trait makes it useful in qualitative analysis of substances.
britannica-1911-schlippe-s-salt:
Schlippe salt, also called sodium thioantimoniate, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It takes its name from Schlippe, who lived from 1799 to 1867. One way to make it is to dissolve set amounts of antimony trisulphide, sulphur, and sodium hydroxide in water. A second way fuses a mix of sodium sulphate, antimony sulphide, and charcoal.

That melt is then dissolved in water and boiled with more sulphur. The liquid is filtered and left to dry down by heat. The salt forms large four sided crystals that dissolve with ease in water. Bare salt melts with ease when heated in a dry state. In its water bearing form, damp air coats it with a red film on the skin. It can also join with a second sodium salt to form a paired compound.
britannica-1911-stilt: Stilt is a short bird note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is also given as Long-legged Plover, for reasons the entry calls plain to any eye. The note itself is a stub that sends the reader on to the fuller entry under the heading Stilts. In the hosted text the stub sits at the end of the entries for Stilo and Stilpo. So the page gives the bird's two names and the cross reference, and leaves the full account of the bird to that linked entry.
britannica-1911-sylt:
Sylt is the largest German island in the North Sea, described in a 1911 Britannica entry. It runs near twenty three miles long yet is most often half a mile wide. A broad limb juts east at its middle, seven miles across at that point. It lies off the Schleswig coast in the Prussian province of that name.

Marsh and moor pasture in the centre feed a few thousand sheep in all. The rest is dunes and sand hills that shift west year by year. Some dunes rise one hundred to one hundred and fifty feet high. Its thirty five hundred folk are Frisian by stock and work at fishing and sea trades.
britannica-1911-tafilalt:
Tafilalt is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an oasis of the Moroccan Sahara. It is called the most weighty oasis of that desert land. It lies ten days' trip south of Fez, across the Atlas range. Its folk name means the country of the Filali tribe.

The oasis is famed for its large and luscious dates of fine taste. Skill with dates raised the reigning house of Morocco to power. Since 1648 sultans have sent their spare sons and daughters there. Its folk live not in towns but in lone walled houses. They are warlike and are at war with each other without end. The ruins of old Sagilmasa stretch five miles by the river.
britannica-1911-whitman-walt:
Walt Whitman lived from 1819 to 1892 and was an American poet of fame. The 1911 Britannica life opens at West Hills on Long Island, New York. He was born there on the last day of May in 1819. His stock was mixed English and Holland Dutch on that isle. That stock had farmed and sailed there for more than 150 years.

His father Walter was a farmer and a carpenter by trade. His mother Louisa was the granddaughter of a sea captain. Walt was the second child in a brood of nine in all. The family moved early to Brooklyn, where he spent his youth. His work life was chequered: errand boy, print shop hand, and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anhalt:
Anhalt is a Vicariate Apostolic covering the German Duchy of Anhalt, 860 square miles. On 1 December 1905 it contained 328,029 inhabitants, mostly Protestants, with 13,493 Catholics. The Bishop of Paderborn, as vicar apostolic, names its pastors. There are four parishes, Dessau, Bernburg, Coethen, and Zerbst, plus three missions.

The Grey Nuns from Breslau, the only order in Anhalt, run visiting-nurse establishments in Dessau and Coethen, plus a kindergarten and a school in Coethen. The public schools are state-directed, yet the Church maintains sixteen private schools. Before the Reformation, Anhalt belonged to the bishoprics of Meissen, Brandenburg, and Merseburg. The few Catholics remaining after those dioceses fell received little attention until 1622. In 1719 the Saxon Franciscans established a mission in Dessau, given a chapel in 1805. Missions followed at Zerbst and Coethen. Duke Ferdinand of Coethen and his wife became Catholics at Paris in 1825 and founded a Coethen congregation, raised to a parish in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-const:
Charles Constance Cesar Joseph Mattheu d'Agoult was a French prelate born at Grenoble in 1747 and dead at Paris in 1824. He trained at the Seminary of St. Sulpice in Paris. He became Bishop of Pamiers in 1787. During the Revolution he emigrated, returning to France only after surrendering his bishopric.

His writings were political and financial rather than theological. They include a project for a national bank in 1815 with an explanatory follow-up in 1816. A letter to a Jacobin reflects on the English constitution and the royal charter. A conversation with E. Burke on the interests of Europe's powers appeared in 1814. Four such works are listed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-perra:
An entry on Charles Perrault, the French writer whose fairy tales made him famous. Born in Paris in 1628, he practised law briefly, then became chief clerk in the king's buildings office in 1664. He suggested the Louvre colonnade to his architect brother Claude and persuaded Colbert to fund pensions for writers and scholars. He helped create the Academy of Sciences and served as lifelong secretary of the Academy of Inscriptions.

Elected to the French Academy in 1671, Perrault opened its meetings to the public. His preface to Le siècle de Louis le Grand and his Parallèle des Anciens et des Modernes launched the quarrel of Ancients and Moderns. There he championed modern writers against Boileau and Bossuet. All of it was outshone by his Contes de ma Mère l'Oye of 1697, the Mother Goose tales, retold with a skill that gave them lasting popularity. He died in 1703.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-raymb:
An entry on Charles Raymbault, a French Jesuit missionary and the first Jesuit to die in Canada. Born in France in 1602, he entered the Society of Jesus at Rouen in 1621. He served as procurator, or business manager, of the Canadian mission before being called to Quebec in 1637. In 1640 he was sent with Father Pijart to follow wandering tribes visiting the Hurons, chiefly Nipissings and Algonquins east and north of Lake Huron.

That mission brought harder conditions than work among the Hurons or the Tobacco Nation, but Jesuit generosity soon bore fruit. When the Sauteux asked for priests in 1641, Raymbault went with the future martyr Jogues as far as Sault Ste. Marie, seeking both converts and the fabled passage to the Western Sea. Worn out by fatigue on his return, he was carried to Quebec, where he died in 1643 and was buried beside Champlain, the colony's founder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-perrau:
Claude Perrault, born at Paris in 1613 and dead there in 1688, built the main eastern facade of the Louvre, known as the Colonnade. He succeeded in medicine and anatomy, in architecture, and as an author, though his talent won him much enmity, especially in architecture. As physician and physicist he took his doctorate at the University of Paris. He joined the Academy of Sciences at its founding in 1666 and repeatedly won prizes for physics and chemistry.

Colbert had him translate Vitruvius, and the work fired his enthusiasm for architecture. His Vitruvius with commentary and tables appeared in 1673, with an epitome in 1674. His Ordering of the Five Kinds of Columns followed in 1683. His triumphal arch design for the Rue Saint-Antoine, preferred to Lebrun's and Leveau's, was only partly built in stone. In the Louvre colonnade competition he beat all rivals, even Bernini, and the work occupied him from 1665 to 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-hunolt:
Franz Hunolt, born at Siegen on 31 March 1691 and dead at Trier on 12 September 1746, was the best-loved German preacher of the early eighteenth century. His name appears in Jesuit catalogues as Humold, Hunoldt, and usually Hunolt. At nine he entered his town's Jesuit college, at fifteen studied philosophy at Cologne, took his master of arts, and entered the Society of Jesus there on 18 May. After a two-year novitiate at Trier and a year at Geyst preparing to teach, he taught at Cologne and Aachen gymnasiums to his superiors' complete satisfaction. He directed the junior sodality and showed remarkable oratorical gifts.

After four years of theology and holy orders, he spent most of his third probation year giving popular missions, so great was his preaching fame. He then took the logic chair at Coblenz and made his profession on 15 August 1724.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-barthe:
George-Barthélemy Faribault, a Quebec archaeologist born in 1789, gave his leisure and fortune to Canada's past. Cousin of the founder of Faribault, Minnesota, he schooled himself for law after a Scotch veteran's classroom. He joined the bar in 1811 and fought as a militiaman against the American invasion of 1812. In 1822 he entered the civil service, rising to assistant clerk of the Assembly by 1832.

Faribault spent every free hour gathering Canadian books and papers, and his fine haul of 1,700 rarities burned with Montreal's Parliament House in 1849. Undaunted, he built a second collection, later left to Laval University. His Catalogue of Works on American history, issued at Quebec in 1837, still ranks among the best, and in 1859 he raised Montcalm's long-planned memorial tablet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-victor-:
Orphaned at eight, Henri Victor Regnault worked as a drapery clerk in Paris while studying in spare hours until he entered the École Polytechnique in 1830. He moved from organic chemistry, where he built new compounds by substituting chlorine for hydrogen, into physics. In 1843 the French government charged him with measuring the properties of steam for engineers. Published in 1847, those results won him the Rumford Medal and the post of Chief Engineer of Mines.

Regnault's reputation rests on exact measurement: specific heats of solids, liquids, and gases, vapour tensions, latent heats, expansion coefficients, and a correction to Mariotte's law of gases. Two laws on the specific heat of gases bear his name, and his tables became standards for engineers and chemists. Directing the Sèvres porcelain works from 1852, he lost laboratory, instruments, and papers in the Franco-German War, a blow compounded by his son's death and a stroke in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-arcadel:
Jacob Arcadelt was a noted musician born in Holland around 1500. He died probably at Paris between 1570 and 1575. He grew up under Josquin and the Belgian school. He began as a singer at Florence's court. In 1539 he went to Rome. He became singing master of St Peter's boys' choir. The next year he joined the papal choir as a singer. He stayed there until 1549.

In 1555 Cardinal Charles of Lorraine engaged his services. Arcadelt followed him to Paris and likely stayed there until death. He was known then as regius musicus, or court musician. Most of his many works were published. Foremost are six books of five-voice madrigals, issued at Venice from 1538 to 1556. Each book holds at least forty pieces. The entry presents a Franco-Flemish master of the madrigal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Faribault, a trader and early settler of Minnesota, was born in Lower Canada in 1774 and died at Faribault, Minnesota, in 1860. His father, a Paris lawyer turned Canadian notary, had served the French army in Canada. After schooling and shop work at Quebec, the son joined the Northwest Fur Company.

From Mackinac in 1798 Faribault traded for a decade with Potawatomi, Dakota, and Sioux peoples along the Des Moines and Minnesota rivers. He settled at Prairie du Chien in 1809, trading on his own account and swapping lead with Julien Dubuque. Refusing to join the English in the War of 1812 cost him jail and his goods, yet he stayed and helped found a frontier town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-bertrand:
Léon Foucault, a French physicist born in Paris in 1819 and dead there in 1868. He showed mechanical genius as a boy, building a boat, a telegraph, and a working steam engine. He quit medicine, unable to bear blood, and worked as preparator for Donné's microscopy course, patching his thin maths training as he went.

In 1845 Foucault took charge of science coverage at the Journal des Débats, won the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1850, and in 1855 became physicist of the Paris Observatory. His turning mirror settled light's speed in different media and overturned the particle theory of light. His pendulum, proving Earth's spin, made his name known far beyond laboratories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-and-abb:
Fontevrault, a double monastery founded by Robert d'Arbrissel near the end of 1100, placed monks and nuns under an abbess in a wooded valley near the Loire. Its rule drew on John's words Behold thy Mother, but practical sense also counted: able nuns, not the feeble brethren around Robert, could govern.

The long line of capable abbesses justified the choice, and Fontevrault led the double orders before Gilbertines and Bridgettines copied its form. The entry compares their rules, traces the abbey's lands, prisons, and royal burials, and follows it to suppression in the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-gibaul:
Pierre Gibault was a Canadian missionary and patriot priest of Illinois, born at Montreal in 1737. Educated at Quebec Seminary and ordained on 19 March 1768, Bishop Briand sent him as vicar-general to Illinois. In July he reached Michilimackinac, spent a week serving Catholics long without a priest, and by September settled at Kaskaskia, later living at Ste. Genevieve, Vincennes, and Cahokia.

At Vincennes in February 1770 he found religion deplorable, converted a Presbyterian family in two months, revived Catholic practice, and that year blessed the little wooden chapel at Paincourt, today's St. Louis. Long the only priest in Illinois and Indiana, he swayed Kaskaskia and Cahokia to submit to George Rogers Clark in 1778 and swear allegiance to Virginia. As Clark's volunteer agent he then won Vincennes to the American cause. In 1791 he retired beyond the Mississippi. He died at New Madrid about 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph:
Pierre-Joseph Desault rose from a poor boyhood in Franche-Comté to become the leading surgeon of Paris in his day. He was born at Magny-Vernois in 1744 and schooled by Jesuits. He left priestly studies for medicine and learned from a village barber-surgeon. He opened his own anatomy school in Paris in 1766 while still under twenty.

His hands-on teaching drew three hundred pupils. He went on to head surgery at the Charity Hospital and the Hôtel-Dieu. He founded a school of clinical surgery that drew students from far afield. His writings covered operations and fractures and dislocations, and he died from pneumonia in 1795 after a brief imprisonment during the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-in:
A Pontifical Indult is a general faculty, or permission, granted by the Holy See to bishops and others to do something the common law does not allow. General needs, peculiar local conditions, and the impossibility of applying to Rome case by case justify such concessions. They run for a set term of three, five, or ten years, or for a set number of cases.

Indults are personal, to be used by the bishop himself or his vicar-general unless he may pass them on, and they differ from dispensations, which cover one particular case only. In a wider sense indult means any privilege, grace, or favour. The entry lists examples. They run from the Lenten indult and an indult of secularisation to leave a religious order, to an indult for a private oratory or a privileged altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salt:
Salt, used since ancient times to season food and keep things from rotting, early gained a sacred character. Elisha sweetened a well's waters with it, eastern peoples rubbed it on a newborn child's skin, and strewing it on land dedicated the ground to the gods. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia moves from Scripture through Jewish law to the Roman Rite.

Jewish sacrifices and the loaves of proposition required salt, and in Matthew's Gospel salt stands for wisdom, perhaps once with a power against evil. In church use, which belongs only to the Roman Rite, two kinds appear. Baptismal salt, cleansed and blessed with exorcisms and prayers, is given to the catechumen before entering church. Blessed salt serves other rites. A canon of Carthage suggests catechumens received it several times a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Ebelholt, also called William of Paris and of the Paraclete, reformed Danish religious life from a Paris canonry. Schooled by his uncle Hugh, forty-second abbot of St-Germain-des-Prés, he was ordained subdeacon and given a canonry at Ste-Geneviève-du-Mont. His exemplary life displeased his fellow canons, who slandered him to block his diaconate from Paris's bishop.

He obtained the order from Senlis's bishop through his uncle, and was presented to the little priory of Epinay. In 1148 Eugene III replaced Ste-Geneviève's secular canons with regular canons from St Victor, and William joined the new community as sub-prior. There he defended regular observance against an irregularly appointed prior, winning papal support. Sent to Denmark, he became abbot of Ebelholt, dying there on Easter Sunday 1203.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-perau:
William Perault was a French Dominican writer and preacher mistaken for Archbishop of Lyons. Born at Perault in France, he died at Lyons on a disputed date, some placing it before 1260, others about 1270 or 1275. He studied at Paris, where preaching, perhaps by Jordan of Saxony, drew him to the Dominicans. Custom sent him to Lyons convent for a life both contemplative and active, famed for writings, preaching, and virtue.

For ten years Perault discharged every episcopal task for Lyons during its vacancy, chosen by Philip of Savoy, who held the archbishop's title from 1245 to 1267 without orders. Hence men called Perault bishop, and a later hand added the title to his books, though Gerson, Echard, and Hurter insist he never held the see. His works include the Summa on virtues and vices, sermons on seasons and saints, a guide for religious, and a rule for princes partly by Aquinas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-xavier-barbie:
Xavier Barbier de Montault was a French archaeologist and liturgist of vast learning. Born at Loudun in 1830, he died at Blaslay in 1901. From a noble family, he was entrusted at eight to his great-uncle, Bishop Montault des Isles of Angers. He read theology at Saint Sulpice, then theology and archaeology at Rome's Sapienza. Ill health sent him home in 1857 as historiographer of Angers diocese, where he mined archives, studied inscriptions, and founded a museum.

A Roman stay from 1861 to 1875 deepened his liturgy lore, served bishops as consultor, and set him as theologian to Bishop Desflèches at the Vatican Council. His first study appeared in 1851 in Annales Archéologiques, and Didron charged him with its index. He poured articles into Revue de l'Art Chrétien until 1903, and in 1889 began reprinting his works, planning sixty volumes but reaching sixteen, prized more for erudition than edge.
collected-poems-1897-1907-by-henry-newbo:
Collected Poems 1897–1907, by Henry Newbolt, is a volume of sea and school verse with a strong patriotic strain. Drake's Drum sounds its best known note. Drake lies in his hammock, dreaming of Plymouth Hoe, till the great Armadas come. His drum, hung by the shore, will call him back to drum the foe up the Channel as before.

The Fighting Téméraire gives a ship her own chorus, sung by the gunner's lads as they polish every gun. A longer poem walks the road of England's wars, from Trafalgar to Torres Vedras and Vigo Bar. Its voice charges a race of tireless fighters not to forget the fame they owe their fathers.
doe-osti-17010319-development-of-integra:
Final report for the DISCOVR algae project at Arizona State University covers work from November 2022 through September 2025. John McGowen led the team at the Arizona Center for Algae Technology and Innovation, under Energy Department award DE-EE0010411. DISCOVR is a national consortium led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory that tests algae strains and growing methods outdoors.

Arizona State served as the main outdoor growing partner, running set protocols in place since 2013. Its trials fed yearly national figures for algae biomass output and checked gains found by other partners. The report covers only the Arizona share of the consortium work, not the results of every partner site.
doe-osti-17076359-status-on-ornl-activit:
Nidia Gallego and Jisue Braatz of Oak Ridge National Laboratory report in September 2026 on molten salt creeping into nuclear graphite. Salt that soaks into graphite pores can change its strength and heat behavior, so reactor designers need to know how far and how fast it spreads. Their test salt was FLiNaK, a mix of lithium, sodium, and potassium fluorides.

Neutron tomography imaged the same graphite sample before and after salt exposure at 750 degrees under pressure. Subtracting the paired 3D images maps the salt directly. Six graphite grades were tested at 12 and 336 hours. Medium grained grades filled throughout quickly, while fine grained grades took salt slowly and only near exposed surfaces.
doe-osti-2588544-comstock-measure-docume:
Chris CaraDonna of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this measure documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95004, dated September 2025. It defines one scenario inside ComStock, the laboratory's bottom-up model of the United States commercial building stock. The scenario applies rooftop solar panels across that stock. Coverage is set at 40 percent of roof area.

ComStock's baseline represents the commercial building stock as it stood in 2018. It was built from data sources, statistical sampling, and building energy simulation, after a three-year calibration effort. A measure is a what-if applied to that baseline. This document specifies how the solar measure is modeled, including utility rates. Rather than presuming one rate, several rates from each model's census tract are simulated. The public dataset carries the minimum, median, mean, and maximum of those rates. Results are published openly, down to county-level custom aggregations, covering energy use, bills, and carbon emissions.
doe-osti-2997593-summary-of-savannah-riv:
Kimberly Crapse and Thomas Peters sum up a year of salt waste qualification data, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2025-00489 dated October 2025. Tanks 21H, 41H, and 42H blend feed for the Salt Waste Processing Facility, which strips cesium from tank waste before disposal. Batches 10 through 13 were qualified for processing during fiscal year 2024.

Samples showed no surprises: no heavy solids, nothing floating, and no odd colors. Chemistry matched earlier batches closely. Quick analyses, done in about four weeks, came from the site contractor's laboratory for the first time across all four batches; the national laboratory supplied the longer eight-week analyses. Tables report values such as methyl mercury and total organic carbon per batch. Operators can send these batches through the plant on this record.
doe-osti-2998825-property-measurements-o:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/CFCT-25/22, by L Gardner, E Dowding, J Rojas and co-workers, measures key properties of a molten salt called FLiNaK. The salt mixes lithium, sodium and potassium fluorides and is a candidate coolant for advanced reactors. Real salt in service picks up rust-like corrosion products and dissolved oxygen, so the team added measured amounts of chromium, nickel and uranium fluorides, plus oxygen-bearing uranium fluoride.

Using scanning calorimetry, an instrument that tracks heat as samples warm, they measured melting behaviour and specific heat. Chromium and nickel fluoride additions lowered the melting range against clean salt. Uranium fluoride with oxygen raised the melting end point. Extra phase changes appeared in doped samples that clean salt lacked. For specific heat, most doped salts matched clean salt within measurement error, while nickel-bearing salt differed clearly. Two calorimetry methods still disagree somewhat, and checking them continues.
doe-osti-3002984-frequency-and-time-mult:
Alex Fischer and Nils Thomas Otterstrom tackle a quantum optics bottleneck in Sandia report SAND2025-13936R, dated November 19, 2025. Photonic quantum computers need many photons at once, yet single photons arrive only by chance, heralded after the fact. Multiplexing attacks that problem: try many generation chances, then switch one success into the output.

The scheme here multiplexes in both frequency and time. Photons occupy several frequency modes within one spatial-temporal mode. Variable-length optical delays reshape the timing, and spaced fiber Bragg grating reflectors steer frequency and time together. Two hardware paths are pursued, one using a free-space optical quantum memory with adjustable delays. The report calculates multiphoton generation rates with losses included, giving builders a realistic yield estimate.
doe-osti-3014774-conjugate-heat-transfer:
Heat flow inside salt-filled fuel pins is modeled in ANL/NSE-25/78, an Argonne report dated September 30, 2025, written with Moltex Energy Canada for the GAIN program. The Stable Salt Reactor seals recycled nuclear waste in narrow salt-filled pins, cooled by liquid salt, so heat must cross the molten fuel salt and cladding reliably for safe operation. Jun Fang led the author team.

The team ran conjugate heat transfer simulations in NekRS, a spectral element code, capturing natural convection inside the pin and forced convection in the coolant under steady and transient conditions. Peak Rayleigh numbers near 6.4 times ten to the fourteenth place the flow firmly in the turbulent natural convection regime. Time-averaged results feed comparisons with RANS models and reduced-order models in the SAM system code for fast safety analysis.
doe-osti-3029103-functional-characteriza:
Breeanna R Urbanowicz of the University of Georgia led this project on the enzymes that build plant carbohydrates, with Yannick Bomble, Pradeep Prabhakar, and others. Glycosyltransferases stitch sugars into nearly every complex carbohydrate, yet most of their functions are unassigned. Duckweed, a small fast-growing aquatic plant and candidate energy crop, served as the model. The team combined high-throughput biochemistry, proteomics, and computation to assign those functions.

Data flowed into deep learning frameworks trained to predict glycosyltransferase function from sequence and context. A structural thread studies the GT47 family in Spirodela polyrhiza by solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance, with samples prepared for the EMSL facility. The method reads cell wall architecture in place, in muro, without extracting the polymers, capturing structure, interactions, and mobility of the wall polysaccharides at atomic detail.
doe-osti-3366049-final-scientific-techni:
Alpha-En Corporation's final report for DOE SBIR award DE-SC0024052, led by Landon Oakes and covering July 2023 to April 2026, demonstrates pulling lithium metal straight out of brine. The Reductive Lithium Extraction process moves lithium ions from brine through a selective membrane. It deposits them as thin-film metal anodes for high-energy batteries. That skips the carbonate intermediate the industry ships around the world. Federal share was 1,352,572 dollars.

Extraction efficiency topped 50 percent from purified brine feedstocks. A 20-micrometer electrode, the commercial thickness benchmark, came out uniform with average areal capacity of 4.15 milliamp-hours per square centimeter, plus or minus 4.3 percent. RLE metal matched or beat commercial controls in coin and pouch cells, including third-party tests. Two generations of roll-to-roll coating prototypes were built and run.
doe-osti-3419449-suli-report-development:
Idaho report INL/RPT-26-94798, dated August 2026, describes a molten salt circulation loop built for live spectroscopy. Daniel Benadof of Purdue wrote the SULI report, with Ammon Williams of Idaho as mentor. The loop supports non-proliferation checks on molten salt reactors.

Salt flows through cells where ultraviolet-visible and laser breakdown methods can read it. A venturi partly aerosolizes the flow before a nebulizer tank. Argon gas then fully aerosolizes the salt for laser tests. Aerosols pass an optical cell and are collected after reading. Live chemical reads could flag diverted material without stopping a reactor.
doe-osti-3683869-fy26-progress-on-demons:
Argonne report ANL/NEAMS-26/3, dated September 11, 2026, tracks Fiscal Year 2026 progress on modelling core bowing in sodium-cooled fast reactors. Five authors are printed: Nicholas Wozniak, Gang Yang, Kyle Ramey, Yiqi Yu, and Emily Shemon. Core bowing is the slight bending of fuel assemblies under uneven heat and radiation. It feeds back on reactivity, so it acts as a passive safety trait. A MOOSE-based workflow joins transport, flow, heat, and mechanics codes to predict it.

New Griffin features drive this year's work, notably sodium backfill and pin power rebuilding on bent shapes. Backfill checks matched hand calculations exactly, with mass conserved. Pin power checks across one, seven, and nineteen assemblies agreed best where leakage was low. The duct-based treatment cost far less computing time. A coupled run at full power gave steady, physical feedback from expansion and bowing.
doe-osti-3684036-zprd-database-zppr-15-m:
Gerardo Aliberti's report gathers Monte Carlo results for the ZPPR-15 experiments into the ZPRD database. ZPPR-15 was a mockup of a 330 megawatt electric Integral Fast Reactor. Its core had two zones, a depleted uranium blanket, sodium cooling, and a steel reflector. The programme ran in four phases, A through D.

Every loading in the database was rerun with MCNP version 6.2 on Argonne's VTR cluster. Each run used three nuclear data libraries in turn, drawn from the ENDF/B-VII and ENDF/B-VIII series. The newer library had to be installed on the cluster for this work, with a later fix for boron-10 data. Tables list the computed eigenvalue and its spread for each loading and library. Sections trace how much of each shift comes from one isotope at a time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CakebreadWalt_C:
Jack White, the Fort Worth photo analyst who spent decades on the Kennedy evidence, wrote this piece on a ballistics claim by a California researcher, Walt Cakebread. Its target is the stretcher bullet theory, part of the single-bullet account at the center of the Warren Report.

The single-bullet theory holds that one bullet wounded both Kennedy and Governor Connally, and the nearly pristine bullet found on a Parkland stretcher is its most contested exhibit. Cakebread's discovery, as White presents it, says that story may be a lie. The piece is assassination-research literature in its native form: an attack on one exhibit, argued in detail.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Jeffrey T. Richelson edited this briefing book, number 590, published in May 2017. It highlights the Archive's Cyber Vault collection by naming more than forty primary sources that every cyber student needs. The list works as a guided entry point into a large archive.

Primary sources on cyber history are scattered across agencies and decades. A curated set of forty-odd documents gives a newcomer the founding papers in one place: early warnings, key decisions, and program records. Teachers and students can use the selection as a syllabus core, then follow its threads into the wider Cyber Vault holdings.
miss-gibbie-gault:
Kate Langley Bosher, the author of Mary Cary, set this novel in a small Southern town. Its first chapter convenes the Guild of Gossips. Miss Gibbie's views, announced in chapter two, drive the talk of the town. Mary Cary herself speaks in later chapters and puzzles over events.

Chapters follow Peggy and her party, a bargain, and a grateful convalescent. A forgotten engagement, a testimony party, and a sudden change build the complications. The ending chapters are titled The Surrender and A Tie That Binds. Bosher writes warmly about a formidable spinster whose sharp tongue hides a generous heart.
nasa-tm-19680006180-semiconductor-switch:
James Vrancik, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, weighed a new kind of electrical switch for spacecraft. His subject is semiconductor switches for alternating-current power in aerospace use. Unlike mechanical switches, these have no moving parts to wear or bounce.

Vrancik studied several static switches built from different devices. He tracked power loss, distortion, leakage, and heat effects in each. The promised gains are high reliability, long life, and resistance to shock and vibration. His team designed and built a breadboard three-phase switch for space use. They tested it starting a fuel pump motor, and found its power loss small.
nasa-tm-19680007863-polarization-measure:
Donald F. Heath, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, measured the day glow of the high air in January 1968. He watched light from oxygen atoms and nitrogen in the far ultraviolet. He checked both how bright the glow was and whether its light waves lined up in one plane.

They did not line up at all, for either the oxygen or the nitrogen light. That plain fact, Heath argues, proves the glow is lit by particles bumping into each other. He then matches the brightness he saw against values worked out from theory. For the oxygen glow, the match is excellent, he reports.
the-tryal-of-william-penn-william-mead-f:
The Tryal of William Penn and William Mead concerns a tumult at the Old Bailey in September 1670. It is transcribed here from the Compleat Collection of State Tryals. That collection was first published in 1719, and this edition is by Don C. Seitz. His foreword declares that liberty, equality, and fraternity were preached through all time. Yet William Penn, the Quaker, came nearer establishing that trinity than any other human before or since. The edition is dedicated to the memory of Thomas Jefferson, 'which needs frequent refreshing.'

Penn and Mead were tried for preaching to a London crowd after their meeting house was shut. The jury's refusal to convict became a landmark of jury independence. The defendants published the account themselves, as the title page proudly says, 'Done by Themselves.' Readers get a founding document of religious liberty in courtroom form.
theodore-roosevelt: Edmund Lester Pearson wrote a life of Theodore Roosevelt for the True Stories of Great Americans series, published by Macmillan in New York in 1920. A frontispiece photograph shows Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill, credited to Underwood and Underwood. Other Pearson titles are listed, from The Believing Years to The Librarian at Play. This record presents the title pages and that portrait only, so Pearson's biography itself is not shown here.
waltoniana-inedited-remains-in-verse-and: Richard Herne Shepherd edited Waltoniana, the unprinted remains in verse and prose of Izaak Walton. Walton wrote The Complete Angler. Shepherd issued the book at London in 1878, with his own notes and preface. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and the first line of that preface only, so the remains themselves are not shown. The contents run by year from 1633 to 1683. They name an elegy on Dr. Donne and lines on Donne's portrait. Verses, an epitaph on Walton's second wife Anne Ken, and letters follow.
westerfelt:
Will N. Harben published the novel Westerfelt with Harper and Brothers in 1901. The story opens in a mountain home after a day of quilting. Two older sisters, Mrs. Slogan and Mrs. Dawson, have had neighbor women in to sew. They take the bright quilt from its frame as the sun goes down.

Harben draws the sisters with care, one sharp in speech and one softened by loss. Talk of fairs and rival quilts sets the local world in place. The scene gives readers a slow, warm start in a small rural town. Speech, work, and kin ties carry the early pages.
